To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

malaria in Sri Lanka is highly variable in space and time, that the prediction of the number of malaria case counts is difficult, and that the addition of rainfall as covariate to the prediction models does not significantly improve prediction of the number cases of malaria.
the best model for forecasting malaria cases in each district in Sri Lanka varies and prediction accuracy is low.

the heterogeneity of malaria patterns in Sri Lanka requires regional specific prediction models; that the prediction error is large at a minimum 22% (one of the districts) at one month ahead predictions; and that the modest improvement made in the short term prediction by the addition of rainfall as covariate to the prediction models may not justify the investment in a forecasting system which would require rainfall data to be processed routinely.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of malaria cases in Sri Lanka, and the results suggest that a forecasting system is not likely to be useful for malaria control.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
malaria forecasting in Sri Lanka is not yet ready to be implemented in a practical setting.
there is a strong need to invest in a system for malaria forecasting in Sri Lanka, but that the present study does not provide a clear indication of how to proceed.
there is a need for further research on malaria prediction in SriLanka.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the malaria control programme in Sri Lanka should continue to invest in strengthening the surveillance system and in improving its capacity for rapid response, rather than invest in a short-term prediction system for malaria.
the current data are insufficient to develop an accurate forecasting system for short term malaria predictions in Sri Lanka.
the prediction of malaria in Sri Lankan districts is not sufficiently accurate for it to be useful in malaria control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prediction models for malaria in Sri Lanka are still in their infancy, and that further research and development is required to make them more useful for the control programmes.

the development of a forecasting system for Sri Lankan malaria requires the identification of specific patterns of malaria in each district and a better understanding of the role of rainfall in the epidemiology of malaria in each of these districts.
the development and use of a forecasting system should be based on a thorough assessment of the prediction error of the models in the specific context of the malaria control programme.
